Silk
SILK
noun
Through the Saxon seolc from the Latin sericum, the cloth of the Seres, the far eastern people from whom the fibre came — a name that carried its own distance and cost in it.

Biblical Definition

Silk is the fine lustrous thread reeled from the cocoon and woven into the costliest of cloths, brought into Israel from far countries and priced accordingly. In the Authorized Version it appears only a handful of times, and every appearance is loaded. Twice it is the LORD’s own gift to His bride: in Ezekiel’s parable Jerusalem is the abandoned infant whom God washes, clothes, and adorns — “I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk” (Eze 16:10), until she was “exceeding beautiful” and prospered into a kingdom (Eze 16:13). Every thread of her splendour was given her. Once it is the honourable dress of a diligent woman: the virtuous wife of Pro 31, whose hands seek wool and flax and whose clothing is silk and purple — the cloth is not condemned, for it is the fruit of her own industry and the credit of her husband in the gates. And once it lies in the cargo of a doomed city: “the merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet” (Rev 18:12), which no man buyeth any more. So silk stands between two poles. Received as God’s gift it clothes a bride; loved for itself it becomes the freight of Babylon.

Webster 1828 Definition

The fine glossy thread spun by the silkworm, and the costly cloth woven of it; in Scripture a gift bestowed upon the bride and a staple of Babylon’s merchandise.

expand to see more

SILK, n. [Sax. seolc; L. sericum, from Seres, the eastern people who first furnished it.] The fine soft thread produced by the silkworm, and the cloth manufactured from it.

It is remarkable for lustre, strength, and lightness, and has always been ranked among the most costly of stuffs.

Anciently brought overland from the east at great charge, whence its use marked royalty and wealth.

In Scripture the clothing bestowed upon Jerusalem in the parable of Eze 16, and part of the merchandise of Babylon (Rev 18:12).

Also the dress of the virtuous woman of Pro 31:22, whose clothing is silk and purple.

Key Scripture

Eze 16:10 — "I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk."

Eze 16:15 — "But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown, and pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by; his it was."

Pro 31:22 — "She maketh herself coverings of tapestry; her clothing is silk and purple."

Rev 18:12 — "The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble,"

Modern Corruption

Silk is claimed as proof-text by two opposite errors: the prosperity preacher who reads Pro 31:22 as a mandate for luxury, and the ascetic who reads Rev 18:12 as a ban on any fine thing at all.

expand to see more

The prosperity teaching seizes on Eze 16 and Pro 31 and argues that God clothes His people in silk, therefore fine living is the birthright of faith and want is the mark of unbelief. The argument dies on the next verses. Ezekiel’s silk is prologue to the most terrible indictment in the prophets: “thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown” (Eze 16:15). The gift became the occasion of the sin, because she began to read it as a wage rather than a mercy, and the chapter ends in the stripping of everything the opening bestowed. That is not a promise of luxury; it is a warning about what luxury does to a heart that forgets who gave it. At the other pole stands the reflex that treats any costly thing as sin in itself, and here Pro 31:22 stands in the way — the woman whose clothing is silk and purple is the woman the chapter praises, whose hands hold the distaff, whose candle goeth not out by night, and who stretcheth out her hand to the poor. Scripture never made poverty a virtue nor wealth a proof.

The dividing line runs through Rev 18. Babylon’s sin was not that silk existed in her warehouses but that her whole life was freight — buying and selling, and the souls of men reckoned as the last item on the manifest. When the city falls, the merchants weep, and they weep for their trade, not for the dead. So the question the word puts to us is never simply what we wear but what we are holding. Receive fine things as Ezekiel’s foundling received hers — as sheer gift to one who had nothing and deserved less — and they will not ruin you. Trust in them, price your standing by them, spend your years accumulating them, and you are already in the cargo lists of a city that is coming down in one hour.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The costliest imported cloth of the ancient world — in Scripture the bride’s bestowed adorning and Babylon’s unsellable freight.

expand to see more

Silk — Saxon seolc, Latin sericum, the cloth of the Seres.

Hebrew meshi, a costly drawn-out stuff (Eze 16:10, 13); Greek sirikon (Rev 18:12).

Every Old Testament use is bestowed clothing — given, not earned.

Eze 16 gives it and Eze 16:39 strips it away again when the bride turns harlot.

In Rev 18:12 it stands third in Babylon’s manifest, which ends with “slaves, and souls of men.”

Usage

"Ezekiel’s silk was a gift to a foundling — every thread of it, and she forgot the giver."

"Pro 31 praises a woman clothed in silk and purple: Scripture makes poverty no virtue and wealth no proof."

"Babylon’s sin was not owning silk but being freight — her manifest ends with the souls of men."
